ACH is directly implementable as an amendable council hypothesis-testing protocol; unlike plain debate it requires an explicit alternative set, an evidence-by-hypothesis matrix, diagnosticity and inconsistency judgments, sensitivity checks, and observable update indicators.

A Key Assumptions Check is directly implementable as a council assumption-audit protocol; unlike plain debate it requires a written analytic line, an explicit stated-and-unstated assumption ledger, fragility and consequence ratings, and named indicators and review dates.

Devil's Advocacy is directly implementable as a protected council challenge protocol for one dominant view; unlike plain debate it requires a commissioned strongest countercase, protected access and airtime, a mandatory written response, and adjudication of what changed.

Team A/Team B is directly implementable for two or more already-strong competing views; unlike plain debate it requires separate teams, a common evidence packet, symmetric resources, independent products, cross-critique, and neutral synthesis without forced consensus.

A premortem is directly implementable after a council has a provisional plan; unlike plain debate it requires a forced failure frame, silent independent cause generation, a risk-to-mitigation register, owners, and observable tripwires.

ICD-203 is directly implementable as a cross-cutting council product-acceptance wrapper, not as a standalone debate; it requires source-quality disclosure, calibrated uncertainty, evidence-assumption separation, alternatives, logical argument, change tracking, accuracy review, training, and independent product evaluation.

All six are implementable as council blueprints, but none is merely 'better debate': ACH, KAC, Devil's Advocacy, Team A/Team B, and premortem are bounded session protocols, while ICD-203 is a cross-cutting acceptance and learning wrapper. Each adds persistent state, specialized roles, mandatory artifacts, and a stop or update rule that the defined plain-debate baseline lacks.

When plugin.json and the marketplace entry disagree on version, plugin.json wins. Disagree fixture pin plugin.json=0.2.0 vs marketplace=9.9.9 resolves to honoured_version=0.2.0 (source=plugin.json). That is the trap: bumping only marketplace.json ships nothing.

When both files pin the same version (0.2.0), the detector reports precedence_signal=false. A one-field marketplace mutation to 9.9.9 makes the same detector fire. Identical versions produce no precedence signal at all.

Whether the win is silent is version-skewed: current docs say `claude plugin validate` warns when marketplace and plugin.json versions differ, while GitHub issue 54280 reported no validate warning. Runtime docs still say Claude Code uses plugin.json without warning at load/update.

Copilot cloud-agent internet access is limited by a firewall that operates only inside the GitHub Actions appliance, only on processes started via the agent's Bash tool, and is configured from GitHub organization/repository Internet-access settings that an organization can lock so repositories cannot override.

Repository administrators can toggle Enable firewall only when the organization-level setting is Let repositories decide; if the org sets Enabled or Disabled, individual repositories cannot change it.

Cloud-agent MCP servers are configured by pasting JSON into the repository settings MCP servers page on GitHub.com and clicking Save MCP configuration; the JSON is not the committed .github/mcp.json used by Copilot CLI.
Copilot cloud agent and Copilot code review only support MCP tools (not resources or prompts) and do not currently support remote MCP servers that use OAuth.

`.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml` is picked up only when the job is named copilot-setup-steps; only steps, permissions, runs-on, services, snapshot, and timeout-minutes (max 59) may be customized, and any other job settings are ignored. fetch-depth on actions/checkout is overridden by the agent.

Repository-wide custom instructions are a Markdown file at `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. The file is used in practice (microsoft/vscode ships one) and is loaded as prompt context by both Copilot cloud agent and Copilot CLI; it is not a server-side admission gate.
Official docs specify repository-wide instructions as `copilot-instructions.md` in the `.github` directory, plus path-specific `NAME.instructions.md` under `.github/instructions`.
Organization custom instructions are entered in the organization Copilot Custom instructions settings text box and saved there; they are not a repository file.
Copilot CLI `--allow-tool` and `--deny-tool` apply only to the current session and are not written to ~/.copilot/permissions-config.json; deny rules still beat allow rules and saved approvals.

Copilot CLI loads MDM managed settings and server-managed settings at startup; MDM wins per key, long-running sessions re-fetch hourly, and keys such as allowedMcpServers / deniedMcpServers / permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode are admin-enforced. An MDM value of disable for disableBypassPermissionsMode always wins.
Cloud agent receives only Agents secrets/variables. Actions, Codespaces, and Dependabot secrets are not passed. MCP config can see only names prefixed COPILOT_MCP_.

The organization policy 'Copilot can search the web' does not apply to Copilot cloud agent even though the cloud agent can access the Internet; assuming that policy is portable across surfaces is a documented error.

Copilot CLI MCP servers are configured in local files (~/.copilot/mcp-config.json, .mcp.json, .github/mcp.json) or via `copilot mcp add`; project files closer to cwd win. This is a client-local loader, distinct from GitHub.com repository MCP settings.

Custom agent profiles are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter (tools, mcp-servers, target). argument-hint and handoffs from VS Code agent files are ignored on github.com cloud agent; mcp-servers is not used in VS Code IDE custom agents.

Temporal names LLM/AI invocations as non-deterministic operations that must be placed in Activities. DBOS requires a workflow function to be deterministic: given the same inputs and the same step return values, it must invoke the same steps with the same inputs in the same order. Azure Logic Apps Until is a condition-terminated loop: the workflow runs inner actions, then evaluates an expression; the loop stops when the expression is true. The engine documents default limits that stop the loop to prevent endless loops.
Until-loop iteration default is 60 (min 1, max 5,000) and timeout default is PT1H on multitenant / stateful single-tenant; stateless single-tenant timeout default is PT5M.

n8n Loop Over Items with Reset plus an If node evaluates an exit condition per iteration. The docs warn that if the termination condition never matches, the workflow execution gets stuck in an infinite loop. The infinite-loop guard is optional: an infinite loop is expressible.

LangGraph cyclic graphs stop on a stop-condition edge or when recursion_limit is exhausted. Exhaustion raises GraphRecursionError, documented as preventing infinite loops. The limit is always present (must be >= 1) and is raisable via config.
Airflow sensors are a condition-terminated wait: they poke until a criteria is met and fail when they time out. timeout is a BaseSensorOperator parameter documented on all sensors.
When BaseSensorOperator.timeout is None, Airflow reads sensors.default_timeout from config. The config template default is 604800 seconds (7 days).

Step Functions has no native Until/While. Condition-terminated iteration is expressed by a Choice state (JSONPath/JSONata rules) looping via Next. Standard executions have a hard quota of 25,000 events in a single execution history; reaching it fails the execution. Maximum execution time is 1 year (Standard) or 5 minutes (Express).

Temporal Workflows may loop on arbitrary conditions in code. Continue-As-New resets Event History so a Workflow can run forever. Workflow Execution Timeout exists but Temporal's Python SDK docs generally do not recommend setting Workflow Timeouts. The iteration/stop guard is optional: an infinite loop is expressible.

Durable Task eternal orchestrations are documented as running indefinitely. continue-as-new resets orchestration history so an infinite loop can run without unbounded history growth. That API is a history-management pattern, not a mandatory stop rule. An infinite loop is expressible and first-class.
Every surveyed engine that can express a condition-terminated loop also installs a mandatory finite iteration cap, so an infinite loop is never expressible.

IBIS/gIBIS graphs with Issue, Position, Argument and supports/objects-to edges admit a mechanical unanswered-rebuttal check (objects-to edge whose attacker has no incoming objects-to) and a mechanical unsupported-position check (position with no supports edge).
Classic six-element Toulmin layouts can be checked for missing Data/Grounds, but unanswered rebuttal is uncheckable: Rebuttal is an unless-circumstance on the warrant, not a reply node.

A Dung AF (AR, attacks) admits a mechanical unanswered-rebuttal check (attack whose attacker is unattacked; cf. Def. 6 acceptability). Native unsupported-claim is uncheckable (no support field). Emitting a faithful AF from council NL is too costly for an agent: it is argument mining, not slot filling.

For this repo's council argument graphs (IMP-0313 typed SUPPORTS/ATTACKS/REBUTS on turns), IBIS is the format that is both mechanically checkable for unsupported claims and unanswered rebuttals and cheap enough for an agent to emit. Toulmin fails the unanswered-rebuttal check; Dung AF fails emit-cost.

extensions.completion_marker_protocol: Literal JSON-permitted U+0085 delimiters preserve one parseable JSON document while Unicode splitlines exposes the exact completion line at tail.
extensions.evidence_requirement_verbatim: two mechanically independent signals per load-bearing claim (rules/common/single-signal-verification.md); every claim carries source lineage (resolved URL + fetch timestamp + sha256 of the fetched bytes), a Sherman-Kent confidence band, and a named independent verification path (_USER-PROMPTS.md:10717); outcomes are resolved from durable artifacts (ledger entries, merged PRs, test results), never from a later summary written by the same agent that made the claim
extensions.prior_stage_output: harvest BLOCKED; two file-only strikes exhausted; pivot to source-level rebuild
extensions.question_or_target: Build a calibration set of >=60 past forward-looking claims from this estate's own artifacts whose outcomes are now known, and measure: for claims tagged 'likely' (55-80 percent), what fraction actually held - and is the harness systematically over- or under-confident?
tests_required_verbatim: detector control: include 5 claims whose outcome is genuinely still unknown and require the pipeline to exclude them rather than score them; scoring an unresolved claim silently biases the calibration
extensions.title: Calibrate Sherman-Kent confidence bands against measured outcomes

maintenance_implication: The likely (55-80%) band is unused on harvested estate claims, while almost-certain dominates tagged contemporaneous facts. Future receipts must emit the five-band lexicon on actually predictive claims. Cloud SUCCESS:delivered without recoverable artifacts must stay UNKNOWN and out of the scored denominator. Unbanded catalog-completion claims can fill a known-outcome set but cannot calibrate a band they do not carry.
